periodic-trends-s1.title: Successive ionization energies of element X
periodic-trends-s1.text: Element X is in period 3. The table gives the energy needed to remove each electron in turn from one mole of gaseous atoms, then ions.

periodic-trends-s2.title: Properties of period 3 elements
periodic-trends-s2.text: Atomic radius, first ionization energy and electronegativity for seven elements in period 3.

items.q: How many valence electrons does X have, and what is the evidence?
options: Five: five ionization energies are listed
Two: the energy roughly triples from the 1st to the 2nd
Three: the energy jumps fourfold at the 4th electron
Four: the 4th energy is the largest one in the outer shell

why.correct: Removing valence electrons costs increasing but moderate energy. The 4th removal is 11,577 kJ/mol, about 4.2 times the 3rd, because it comes from a full inner shell.
options: The table lists five removals, but they are not all from the outer shell.
Each removal costs more as the ion gets more positive; the large jump comes later.
Right: the 4th electron comes from the inner shell, so it takes far more energy.
The 4th electron is the first core electron, which is why its energy is so large.
Aluminum
Magnesium
Phosphorus
Boron
Right: a period 3 element with three valence electrons is in group 13.
Magnesium has two valence electrons, so its jump would come after the 2nd electron.
Phosphorus has five valence electrons; its jump would come after the 5th.
Boron also has three valence electrons, but it is in period 2.

items.q: Why is the 4th ionization energy so much larger than the 3rd?
options: The ion X³⁺ has a full outer shell, which it wants to keep
The 4th electron has a larger charge than the first three
The nucleus gains protons as electrons are removed
The 4th electron is in shell 2, closer and less shielded

why.correct: The first three electrons are 3s and 3p, far out and well shielded. The 4th is a 2p electron: closer, and shielded only by the 1s pair, so it is held far more tightly.
options: Ions do not want anything; the cause is the electron's distance and shielding.
Every electron carries the same charge.
Removing electrons never changes the number of protons.
Right: less distance and less shielding give a much stronger Coulombic attraction.

items.q: What is the total energy needed to remove all the valence electrons from one mole of gaseous X atoms?

mistakes.why: Value: you added all five energies. Only the first three electrons are valence electrons.
Value: that is only the 3rd electron. Add the energies for all three valence electrons.

why.correct: 577.5 + 1816.7 + 2744.8 = 5139.0 kJ/mol. Each value has one decimal place, so the sum keeps one.

items.q: Each successive ionization energy of X is larger than the one before. Why?
options: Each electron removed is closer to the nucleus than the one before
Each comes from an ion that is more positive than before
The atom gains mass after each electron is removed
Later electrons are in s subshells, which are held more tightly

why.correct: After each removal, the same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons, and less electron-electron repulsion remains, so the next electron is held more tightly.
options: The first three come from shell 3; only the jump at the 4th is a change of shell.
Right: the same protons now pull on fewer electrons, with less repulsion among them.
Removing an electron makes the particle slightly lighter, and mass is not the cause.
The 1st electron is 3p and the next two are 3s; that does not explain the steady rise.

items.q: Which explanation accounts for the decrease in atomic radius from Na to Cl?
options: Atoms with more electrons pack their electrons more tightly
Each element across the period fills a new, smaller shell
Heavier atoms are denser and so take up less space
Protons rise while the shell and core electrons stay the same

why.correct: Across a period, protons are added while the core (1s² 2s² 2p⁶) stays the same, so the effective nuclear charge on the valence electrons rises and pulls them closer.
options: Electrons repel each other; more electrons alone would spread out, not shrink.
All seven fill the same valence shell, n = 3.
Mass and density are not causes in Coulomb's law; charge and distance are.
Right: a larger nuclear charge at a similar distance pulls the valence electrons in.

items.q: Al has a lower first ionization energy than Mg, against the trend. Which explanation is best?
options: Al loses a 3p electron, which is higher in energy than 3s
Al has more protons, so it holds its electrons less tightly
Mg has a full 3s subshell, which it wants to keep
Al is a larger atom than Mg

why.correct: The electron removed from Al is a 3p electron, which is higher in energy than a 3s electron and is shielded in part by the 3s pair. Less energy removes it.
options: Right: the 3p electron is held less tightly than Mg's 3s electrons despite one more proton.
More protons would pull harder; something else must outweigh that.
Atoms do not want things; the reason is the energy and shielding of the electron removed.
The table shows Al (143 pm) is smaller than Mg (160 pm).

items.q: Which element in the table attracts shared electrons most strongly?
options: Na
S
Cl
P

why.correct: Electronegativity measures attraction for shared electrons. It rises across a period as nuclear charge rises at similar distance; Cl is highest.
options: Na has the largest radius and lowest electronegativity, 0.93.
S is second highest at 2.58.
Right: it has the highest electronegativity, 3.16.
P has the highest ionization energy among P, Si and Al, but its electronegativity, 2.19, is below Cl's.

items.q: Which claim about the trends in the table is supported by the data?
options: First ionization energy rises at each step across the period
Atomic radius increases with the number of protons
As radius decreases, electronegativity increases
Electronegativity is unrelated to atomic radius

why.correct: Smaller atoms hold electrons, including shared ones, more tightly. Ionization energy has two exceptions, so "every step" is not supported.
options: It dips from Mg to Al (738 to 578) and from P to S (1012 to 1000).
Radius falls from Na (11 protons) to Cl (17).
Right: from Na to Cl, radius falls from 186 to 99 pm while electronegativity rises from 0.93 to 3.16.
The two change together across every step of the table.

items.q: Why is the first ionization energy of potassium lower than that of sodium?
options: K's valence electron is farther out and more shielded
K has more protons, which push the electron away
K has more mass, so its electron moves faster
K is a metal and Na is not

why.correct: Down a group, each element adds a shell. The valence electron is farther from the nucleus and shielded by more core electrons, so it is held less tightly.
options: Right: distance and shielding increase down a group, outweighing the extra protons.
Protons attract electrons; they never push them away.
Mass is not the cause in Coulomb's law.
Both are metals in group 1.

items.q: How does each ion's radius compare with the radius of its own atom?
options: Na⁺ is larger than Na, and Cl⁻ is smaller than Cl
Na⁺ is larger than Na, and Cl⁻ is larger than Cl
Na⁺ is smaller than Na, and Cl⁻ is smaller than Cl
Na⁺ is smaller than Na, and Cl⁻ is larger than Cl

why.correct: Na⁺ has lost its only shell-3 electron, so its outermost electrons are in shell 2 and it is much smaller than Na. Cl⁻ has one more electron than Cl with the same 17 protons; the extra electron-electron repulsion spreads the cloud, so Cl⁻ is larger than Cl.
options: This is the reverse of both changes: losing electrons shrinks a particle and gaining them expands it.
Losing the whole third shell makes Na⁺ smaller than Na, not larger.
Gaining an electron adds repulsion with no added protons, so Cl⁻ is larger than Cl.
Right: a cation is smaller than its atom and an anion larger than its atom.

items.q: O²⁻, F⁻ and Na⁺ each have 10 electrons. Which is smallest, and why?
options: O²⁻, because it has the smallest atomic number
Na⁺, since 11 protons pull on the same 10 electrons
F⁻, because it is in the middle of the three
They are the same size, since they have the same electrons

why.correct: With the same 10 electrons, radius depends on nuclear charge: O (8 protons) > F (9) > Na (11). Na⁺ is smallest.
options: Fewer protons means a weaker pull on the 10 electrons, so O²⁻ is the largest.
Right: same electron arrangement, most protons, so the strongest pull and smallest size.
Size follows proton count here, and F⁻ has fewer protons than Na⁺.
Same electrons, but different nuclear charges, so different sizes.

items.q: Moving down group 2 from magnesium to calcium, predict how each quantity changes.

variables.name: Atomic radius
variables.why: Calcium's valence electrons are in shell 4, farther out than magnesium's shell 3.

variables.name: First ionization energy
variables.why: A farther, more shielded valence electron is held less tightly.

variables.name: Number of valence electrons
variables.why: Both are in group 2, with two valence electrons.

why.correct: Down a group, shells are added: radius rises, ionization energy falls, valence electrons stay the same.

items.q: Fluorine is more electronegative than iodine. Which statements correctly help explain this? Select all that apply.
options: Fluorine's valence electrons are in shell 2, much closer to the nucleus
Iodine's valence electrons are shielded by many more core electrons
Iodine has more protons, so it attracts electrons more strongly
Fluorine has a larger mass than iodine

why.correct: Both atoms have 7 valence electrons. Fluorine's are far closer and less shielded, so its nucleus attracts shared electrons more strongly.
options: Right: shared electrons are closer to fluorine's nucleus.
Right: more shielding weakens the attraction iodine exerts.
More protons, but much more distance and shielding, so the net attraction is weaker.
Fluorine has a much smaller mass, and mass is not the cause anyway.

items.q: Where on the periodic table are the metals?
options: On the left and in the middle
In the top right corner of the table
In group 18, the last column
Along the staircase line

why.correct: Most elements are metals, on the left and in the middle; nonmetals are at the upper right, with metalloids along the staircase between.
options: Right: metals have few valence electrons that are held loosely.
The upper right holds the nonmetals.
Group 18 is the noble gases, which are nonmetals.
The staircase holds the metalloids, which are in between; metals fill most of the table to its left.
